0.0.n: Introduces an example of the point being discussed.

0.2.n: 多く links to 日本人 with の to describe a large number of people.

0.3.n: Connects 多く to 日本人; together they mean many Japanese people.

0.4.n: 人 added to 日本 refers to people from Japan.

0.5.n: Marks Japanese people as the topic of the actions across these lines.

1.0.n: This is the Japanese name or title for Jesus Christ.

1.1.n: Connects Christ to birthday, identifying whose birthday it is.

1.2.n: キリストの誕生日 describes Christmas in the phrase that follows.

1.3.n: Combines with ある to form である, a formal written-style equivalent of だ.

1.4.n: Completes である; the whole preceding phrase describes Christmas as Christ's birthday.

1.5.n: This holiday name is written in katakana because it is borrowed from another language.

1.6.n: Marks Christmas as what people celebrate.

1.7.n: お祝いし is the linking form of お祝いする, connecting this action to the next ones.

2.0.n: Refers to the closing part of the year.

2.1.n: Marks the end of the year as the time of the action.

2.2.n: Highlights this time period, contrasting it with the other occasions mentioned.

2.3.n: お adds a respectful tone to 寺, which refers to a Buddhist temple.

2.4.n: Marks temples as the location where people listen to the bells.

3.0.n: A set expression for Buddhist temple bells traditionally rung 108 times around midnight on New Year's Eve.

3.1.n: Marks the bells as what people listen to.

3.2.n: The て-form of 聞く links listening to the next action.

4.0.n: Introduces the next event in the sequence.

4.2.n: お is a customary polite prefix; 正月 can cover the New Year period, not just January 1.

4.3.n: Marks the New Year holiday as the time of the visit.

4.4.n: Highlights the New Year occasion in contrast with the earlier times.

5.0.n: Refers to Shinto places of worship, unlike the Buddhist temples mentioned earlier.

5.1.n: Marks the shrine as the destination of 行きます.

5.2.m: first shrine visit of the year
5.2.n: Names the customary first New Year visit to a shrine or temple; here, the destination is a shrine.

5.3.n: Marks 初詣 as the purpose of going.

5.4.n: The polite present form of 行く describes a customary action here, rather than one specific future trip.

0.lit: For example, as for many Japanese people,
0.tip: 多くの before a noun means many; は sets up the topic for the whole sentence.

1.lit: Celebrate Christmas, which is Christ's birthday, and,
1.tip: 誕生日である describes the noun immediately after it: Christmas.

2.lit: At year's end, at Buddhist temples,
2.tip: に marks when the action happens, while で marks where it happens.

3.lit: Listen to the New Year's Eve bells, and,
3.tip: 聞いて links this action to the next rather than ending the sentence.

4.lit: And then, as for the New Year holiday,
4.tip: お正月 refers to the New Year holiday period, not necessarily only New Year's Day.

5.lit: Go to Shinto shrines for the first visit of the year.
5.tip: The first に marks the destination; the second に marks the purpose of going.
